chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding an egg that came out from the vent of a dead hen, he said, 'If it was covered with thick skin, there is no harm in it.'

58 - From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn al-Hasan al-Alawi, all from al-Fath ibn Yazid al-Jurjani, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I wrote to him asking him about the skins of a dead animal whose meat is eaten if slaughtered, so he (peace be upon him) wrote back:

'One does not derive benefit from the dead animal by its hide or sinew, and everything that is from the horns/hooves of the wool, if sheared, and the hair, and the coarse hair, and the horn casing, and the horn (one derives benefit from them), and one does not exceed to other parts, God willing.'

key_terms.السِّخَالِ: horns/hooves (specifically referring to the covering or the horn itself in this context)

ai.seo_question: What parts of a dead animal are permissible to use according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinction between the carcass itself and its durable byproducts, ruling that an egg from a dead hen is permissible if it has developed a protective shell, while excluding the hide and sinew of land animals whose meat is edible. It further establishes that materials like wool, hair, horns, and nails are permissible for use, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that certain parts of the dead animal are not considered 'flesh' in the restrictive sense. This ruling is foundational in fiqh al-maytah (jurisprudence of the carcass) for determining what constitutes impurity versus usable material.
